title: Dharma Manikya Writes the Rajmala
subtitle: How a Hill King Bound His People’s Memory into Verse and Water
region: Tripura, Benares, Comilla and the Arakan frontier
moral: A people who record memory can argue honestly with legend.

sources.citation: Rajmala, first canto, attributed to Sukreswar and Vaneswar under Dharma Manikya I
sources.note: Self-referential source for the court chronicle's commissioning.

sources.citation: Dharmasagar tank, Comilla, dated by local tradition to 1458 CE
sources.note: Surviving hydraulic monument attributed to Dharma Manikya.

sources.citation: D.C. Sircar, Studies in the History of India (1979); Ramani Mohan Sarma (1987)
sources.note: Epigraphic and historical framework for the revised early sequence.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of a lone king standing between a vast stepped tank and ghostly scrolls swirling in the sky

dialogue.text: In the fifteenth century, as rivers shifted and kingdoms fought, Dharma Manikya of Tripura did something strange for a warrior king: he stopped to write down his people’s past.

panels.shot: wide aerial shot over dense green hills fading into the plains of Bengal, with faint outlines of rival kingdoms at the horizons

dialogue.text: Around 1430, the Manikya kingdom stood at a crossroads of hills and plains, between Bengal’s sultans, Arakan’s coast, and older Kokborok-speaking chiefdoms rooted in these forests.

panels.shot: medium shot at a riverbank ferry, with the king dismounting and touching the water

dialogue.text: The Rajmala itself remembers him returning from pilgrimage, moving along rivers and roads toward Benares, pausing at shrines and ferries that tied Tripura to the wider world.

panels.shot: wide shot of Benares ghats at dawn, with the king among pilgrims

dialogue.text: In Benares, he would have seen another kind of power: Brahmins with palm-leaf books, lineages recited by heart, histories woven into ritual, binding kings to stories older than their crowns.

panels.shot: close-up on the king’s thoughtful face, light from an oil lamp flickering

dialogue.speaker: dharma_manikya_i
dialogue.text: Our hills remember in song. Who will hear us if the songs are lost?

panels.shot: transition wide shot of the king’s return caravan entering a hill capital

dialogue.text: When he returned to Tripura, he carried more than gifts and merits. He carried a question: how should a hill kingdom, with its own tongue and gods, speak to this new world of chronicles?

panels.shot: interior medium shot in a wooden hall, king seated with two learned poets before him

dialogue.text: The Rajmala names the men he chose: Sukreswar and Vaneswar. Under his order they would shape Tripura’s memories into Bengali verse, drawing from older Kokborok tales and a lost Rajratnakar.

panels.shot: medium shot focused on the king speaking firmly to the poets, with attendants listening

dialogue.speaker: dharma_manikya_i
dialogue.text: Write our line as we remember it, yet in a tongue the plains will read.

panels.shot: montage-style medium shot of scribes at work, with faint overlay of hill bards performing

dialogue.text: Behind their neat lines lay older voices in Kokborok and Koloma script, an oral and written memory already centuries deep, now being recast into Sanskritic frames and Bengali metres.

panels.shot: close-up of a palm-leaf manuscript being unrolled before the king

dialogue.text: The first canto of the Rajmala took shape at his court, tracing Manikya origins and conquests. Its kings are real, its pride clear, but its early genealogy is tangled and often at odds with other evidence.

panels.shot: medium shot of the king in discussion with priests and elders around the manuscript

dialogue.text: Even at the moment of writing, memory was being argued: lineage stretched, ancestors reordered, hill deities aligned with Puranic gods. The Rajmala preserved, but it also reshaped, what came before.

panels.shot: wide conceptual shot showing a timeline fading into mist with later hands revising earlier scrolls

dialogue.text: Later cantos would alter the early tale, adding episodes, smoothing defeats, fitting Tripura into changing politics. For modern historians, the Rajmala is a vital witness—and an interested one.

panels.shot: wide shot of the king inspecting the site of the future Dharmasagar tank with engineers

dialogue.text: Tradition in Comilla links the same king to another monument of memory: Dharmasagar, a great tank said to have been completed around 1458, spreading Tripura’s reach into the plains with water and stone.

panels.shot: medium shot of the king kneeling to pick up a handful of soil at the tank site

dialogue.speaker: dharma_manikya_i
dialogue.text: Let this water remember us when words fade.

panels.shot: wide shot of the completed Dharmasagar tank filled with water, lined by steps and trees

dialogue.text: Dharmasagar anchored settlement and ritual, a reservoir that outlived palaces. Archaeology and local memory point back to Dharma Manikya, tying his name to both text and water.

panels.shot: medium shot of the king at court receiving a coastal envoy with a map showing Arakan

dialogue.text: Other traditions, from Arakan, remember him too—as a helper of Min Saw Mon in the struggles of that coastal kingdom. The details are debated, but they show Tripura in a wider Burmese–Bengal theatre.

panels.shot: conceptual wide shot juxtaposing battle standards with a manuscript and a tank

dialogue.text: Dharma Manikya’s campaigns against Bengal’s frontiers have left fewer traces than his chronicle and his tank. Steel rusts quickly; verse and water, when tended, endure in quieter ways.

panels.shot: close-up of a modern researcher’s hands handling an old Rajmala manuscript in a library

dialogue.text: Today, scholars read the Rajmala against inscriptions, Kokborok manuscripts, and oral lore, peeling back layers of courtly revision to glimpse the older Tripura that sang beneath the verses.

panels.shot: final wide shot of the king’s silhouette reflected alongside stars in the Dharmasagar water at night

dialogue.text: By ordering the Rajmala and digging Dharmasagar, Dharma Manikya turned a hill people’s memory into text and stone—so that later generations could argue with legend instead of living only inside it.
